newsitem.title: USA: Iraqi family gave Democrats $400,000 -- paper.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi family gave Democrats $400,000 -- paper.

text.p: An Iraqi-American family wanting sanctions against Iraq eased gave about $400,000 at a fundraiser attended by President Bill Clinton, the Detroit Free Press reported on Monday as controversy over foreign political contributions escalated on the final day of the campaign.

Republican Party Chairman Haley Barbour called the contribution by the Danou family of Bloomfield Township, a Detroit suburb, part of a continuing questionable pattern of contributions made by foreigners -- from a Buddhist nun to Indonesian and Korean businessmen -- to the Democratic Party.

Over the weekend, Republican spokesmen raised questions about a photograph taken at a 1993 fundraiser of Clinton and a Russian, Grigori Loutchansky, who has been accused in press reports of being linked to the KGB and Russian organised crime. The Republicans said Loutchansky even had a private meeting with Clinton.

In his final campaign blitz, Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole hammered away at Clinton for taking foreign contributions, saying at several stops, "In my administration, I will not sell access to the White House."
Democratic campaign spokesmen were not available for comment about the latest allegations.

The Detroit News said the Danou family, headed by businessman Samir Danou, who has lived in the United States since 1965, gave about $400,000 to the Democratic party at a fundraiser they organised at a local movie theatre on Oct. 21 attended by many members of the Chaldean American community. Chaldeans are Christian Iraqis and the Detroit area is home to their largest community outside of Iraq.

The paper quoted Danou's niece Julie Danou as saying the family gave between $400,000 and $500,000 to the Clinton campaign for the purpose of "helping Iraq, to help the people there, to open sanctions."
She said the president in meetings with people attending the private fundraiser promised to work toward lifting the embargo and sending food and medicine to the Iraqi people.

The United Nations, with full U.S. backing and encouragement, has kept sanctions on Iraq since the end of the Gulf War in 1991. Clinton has frequently said easing of sanctions depended on actions taken by Saddam Hussein.
Michigan Dole campaign executive director John Long was quoted by the paper as saying the fundraiser showed "our foreign policy is for sale to the highest bidder."

The Free Press said Samir Danou has been a regular contributor to both the Democratic and Republican parties over the years, giving $1,000 contributions to both Clinton and Dole earlier in the year and donating $25,000 during the last two years to the Republican National Committee.

While Congress has slapped limits on what individuals can donate to presidential candidates, there are no limits on so-called soft money contributions to party organisation work, leading to current concerns about campaign financing.

More than $200 milllion has been contributed, mostly by business interests, to the two parties this year and Fred Wertheimer, a former president of Common Cause, said 1996 has proved to be the worst year ever for campaign finance abuses.
